opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What really draws me to 1X's hardware approach is that it starts from the question of how a robot can safely live and work around people, rather than treating safety as something you bolt on at the end.

A lot of robotics historically has been built for factories, where the robot sits in a cage and people stay out of the way. That leads you toward stiff, heavy, very precise machines. But if you want a robot in a home, next to kids, pets, and furniture, you need something fundamentally different. The emphasis on compliant, low-inertia, softer actuation matters a lot to me. If the robot bumps into you, it should feel more like bumping into a person than into a car door. That changes what's possible. You can let the robot explore, make mistakes, and learn in the real world without every mistake being dangerous or expensive.

As someone who comes from the learning side, I also love that the hardware is designed with data in mind. The humanoid form isn't just aesthetic. Our world is built for human bodies, so a robot with a similar shape can use the same spaces and tools, and it can learn from human demonstrations and teleoperation much more naturally. If you believe, as I do, that the path to general-purpose robots runs through huge amounts of diverse, real-world experience, then you need hardware that's safe enough, robust enough, and eventually affordable enough to deploy at scale. Hardware and AI really have to be co-designed.

Finally, I'm inspired by the vertical integration. Building your own motors and mechanics means you can iterate on the whole system together instead of being bottlenecked by off-the-shelf parts. That tight loop between what the models need and what the body can do is, I think, where a lot of the real progress in embodied AI will come from.

r001.rationale: It describes compliant, low-inertia, softer actuation so bumps are less forceful, and separately notes that 1X builds its own motors and mechanics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find really compelling about 1X is that they've designed the hardware from the ground up to be safe and simple, and that has consequences all the way up the stack.

Most humanoid companies start from the classic robotics playbook: rigid links, high gear ratios, hydraulics or stiff electric actuators. That gives you precision and strength, but it also gives you a machine that's heavy, loud, and genuinely dangerous to be around. 1X went the other direction. Their robots are built around low gear ratio, backdrivable actuators and a soft, lightweight body, so the robot is inherently compliant. If it bumps into you, it gives. That's not a safety layer bolted on in software, it's physics.

Why does that inspire me as a learning person? Because it changes what data you can collect and how you collect it. If the robot is safe enough to be in a home around people, you can actually deploy it, let it operate alongside humans, and gather real-world experience at scale rather than confining everything to a lab cage. The hardware choice unlocks the data flywheel. And compliance also makes the learning problem more forgiving, since small errors in a policy don't turn into broken objects or broken robots.

The other thing I admire is the discipline around cost and manufacturability. They're clearly thinking about building thousands of these, not a handful of demo units. In my experience, the field often underestimates how much progress comes from boring things like reliability and unit economics rather than from a flashy capability. 1X seems to take that seriously, and that's what makes me think they're building for the long game.

r001.rationale: The response says 1X uses low gear ratio, backdrivable actuators and a compliant body so the robot gives when it bumps into someone, making contact itself safer through the hardware.

astra-6.text: What inspires me is the idea that the hardware and the intelligence have to develop together. A robot’s physical design shapes what it can learn, how it interacts with people, and where it can be useful. So I’m excited by an approach that treats those as one problem: building a body and an intelligence that work well together in everyday environments.

r001.rationale: The response discusses developing robot hardware and intelligence together, but does not identify designing motors so robot contact is low impact as a 1X hardware safety approach.

sol-6.1.text:
What inspires me is the willingness to design the hardware around the environment where the robot will actually operate. If you want robots to work alongside people, especially in homes, safety and physical interaction have to be part of the design from the beginning.

And from a learning perspective, hardware and intelligence are deeply connected. The body determines what the robot can experience, what data it can collect, and what kinds of mistakes it can learn from. I find that really exciting: building the body and the intelligence together, so that each can inform the other.

r001.rationale: The response mentions designing for safety and physical interaction, but does not identify designing the motors so that robot contact itself is low impact.
